questions.a: Wind is simply air in motion. A student who answers "a type of gas" or "the weather" is confusing the substance with the action; they need to recall that movement is the defining feature of wind.

questions.q: If a region is very cold, will the air there have high or low pressure?
questions.a: The air will have high pressure. If the student answers "low pressure," they have confused the behavior of cooling (contracting/sinking) with heating (expanding/rising).

questions.q: If City A is hot and City B is cold, in which direction will the wind blow?
questions.a: The wind will blow from City B (cold/high pressure) to City A (hot/low pressure). A wrong answer suggests the student hasn't internalized the "high-to-low" rule.

Warm air expands, which makes it less dense and lighter, causing it to rise above the heavier, cooler air. A wrong answer like "because it is fast" suggests they are guessing rather than understanding density changes.

questions.q: Is air pressure the same everywhere on Earth? Why or why not?
questions.a: No, it varies because temperatures are different in different places, which changes how air behaves. A wrong answer suggests the student thinks the atmosphere is a uniform "blanket" that never changes weight.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment to show that air moves from cold to warm areas.
questions.a: The student should propose placing an incense stick near a heat source (like a lamp) and observing the smoke drift toward the heat. A poor answer fails to include a way to visualize the invisible air movement.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Wind is the movement of air across the Earth's surface, caused by ______ in air pressure that force air to travel from high-pressure areas to low-pressure areas.
Fill in the blank: Have you ever felt a sudden ______ when you open a window, or wondered why a fan makes air move?
What is Wind? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Wind is the movement of air across the Earth's surface, caused by differences in air pressure that force air to travel from high-pressure areas to low-pressure areas.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Wind?
questions.a: Students often believe that "wind creates pressure," when it is actually the opposite: pressure differences create wind.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to explain that wind flows from high-pressure to low-pressure zones and describe how temperature changes (heating/cooling) create these pressure differences.
